opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to clarify is what we mean by "human-level capability," because that phrase gets used very loosely. Today's systems are extremely good at retrieving and recombining patterns they've seen before, and a lot of everyday software engineering *is* that: writing boilerplate, wiring up APIs, translating a well-specified idea into code. That part is already being automated, and it will keep being automated. But that was never really the core of the job.

The core of software engineering is figuring out what to build in the first place. It's taking a messy, ambiguous situation (a business need, a user who can't quite articulate what they want, a system with constraints nobody has written down) and turning it into a precise specification. That's an act of abstraction and adaptation to novelty. If we get systems that can genuinely do that, efficiently, on problems they haven't seen before, then yes, that's a real shift, and we should be honest about it.

Even then, I don't think humans disappear from the loop. I think the role moves up the stack. You go from being someone who writes code to someone who directs intent. You define the goals, you set the constraints, you make the judgment calls about trade-offs, and you verify that what was built actually matches what you wanted. Programming has always moved in this direction. We went from machine code to assembly to high-level languages to frameworks, and each step meant people spent less time on mechanics and more time on what they were actually trying to achieve. AI is a continuation of that trend, perhaps a dramatic one, but still a continuation.

And I'd add that this tends to expand the field rather than shrink it. When you make software dramatically cheaper to produce, you don't end up with less software. You end up with vastly more, built by many more people, for problems that were never worth solving before because the cost was too high. So I expect a lot more people doing something that looks like software engineering, just with a very different toolset and a much greater emphasis on clear thinking, problem formulation, and taste.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a shift toward directing intent and a different toolset, but it does not clearly predict the creation of entirely new interfaces for working with AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the premise needs some unpacking first, because "human-level capability" isn't really one thing. Software engineering is a bundle of very different activities, and AI is reaching human-level on some of them much faster than on others.

If you look at what a programmer actually does, there's a layer of it that is essentially retrieval and interpolation. You know the pattern, you've seen this kind of problem before, you adapt a known solution to a slightly different context. That's the part where models are already extremely good, and honestly for a lot of day-to-day work that's most of the job. Boilerplate, glue code, API plumbing, translating a clear spec into an implementation. I expect that to be almost entirely automated, and fairly soon.

But then there's a different layer, which is dealing with genuine novelty. You're facing a situation that doesn't look like anything in your training distribution, so to speak. Requirements are ambiguous or contradictory. The system has emergent behavior nobody anticipated. You have to figure out what the problem even is before you can solve it. That's where I think humans remain central for quite a while, because that's fluid intelligence, that's on-the-fly program synthesis in your head rather than pattern matching. And it's precisely the thing current deep learning struggles with, which is what ARC was designed to measure.

So my picture of software engineering in the near future is that the human role shifts upward in abstraction. You become less of a code writer and more of a specifier, an architect, a verifier. You decide what should exist and why. You define the constraints. You evaluate whether what came back actually does what you intended, which is harder than it sounds because the model will produce something that looks plausible even when it's subtly wrong. The bottleneck moves from generating code to having a precise understanding of what you want and being able to check it.

And I'd add one more thing. Programming as a discipline has always been about automating our own work. Compilers automated assembly. High-level languages automated memory management. Frameworks automated infrastructure. Each time, the number of programmers went up, not down, because the cost of building software dropped and demand expanded to fill the space. I think AI is the next step in that same lineage, a very powerful one, but the same lineage. People who understand how to decompose problems and reason about systems will be more productive by a large factor. The ones who were mostly doing the retrieval part will need to move up the stack. That's a real transition and it will be uncomfortable for some people, but it's not the disappearance of the profession. It's the profession becoming what it was always supposed to be, which is thinking clearly about problems, rather than typing.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a shift in engineers’ roles toward specifying, architecting, and verifying, but does not predict the creation of entirely new interfaces for working with AI.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between automating a task and automating the entire process of deciding what should be done. In software engineering, writing code is only part of the work. You also have to figure out what problem you’re solving, what constraints matter, and whether the thing you built actually meets somebody’s needs.

If AI can write software at a human level, then the interface to software development moves up a level of abstraction. You spend less time specifying individual steps and more time specifying the outcome you want, examining the result, and refining your intent. And that’s already what programming languages have been doing for us: allowing us to express more with less effort.

Now, that doesn’t mean every existing software engineering job stays the same. Some tasks could disappear entirely. But making software cheaper also makes many more projects worth pursuing. People who couldn’t build software before can start creating their own tools.

So I would expect humans to remain involved in a much more iterative process of expressing goals and exercising judgment. The scarce resource becomes less the ability to produce code and more the ability to decide what is worth building.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that the interface to software development will move to a higher level of abstraction, but does not clearly predict the creation of entirely new interfaces for working with AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reaching human-level capability doesn’t mean that humans suddenly have nothing left to contribute. Software engineering is not just translating a specification into code. A great deal of the work is figuring out what the specification should be: What problem are we trying to solve? What constraints matter? How do we know that we’ve built something useful?

If you can automate the implementation, then people can work at a higher level of abstraction. You can explore more ideas, build more ambitious systems, and spend more time understanding what users actually need. But you still need some way to establish that what the machine has produced matches your intent.

Now, if by human-level capability you mean a system that can do absolutely everything a human engineer can do, including choosing goals and navigating an organization, then you’re asking an economic and social question as much as a technical one. There isn’t a technical guarantee that the demand for human labor stays the same. That will depend on how we choose to deploy these systems and distribute the benefits.

r001.rationale: The response says people may work at a higher level of abstraction when implementation is automated, but it does not predict the creation of entirely new interfaces for working with AI.
